sweep_summary: Bora (bora1263) is in the catalog as 'tonal' on Thiesen & Weber 2012 (no stress system apart from tone; possibly stress implemented on tone). All three title-keyword items are the Seifart/Meyer drummed-speech (manguaré) studies: Meyer, Dentel & Seifart 2012 Interspeech (downloaded open from ISCA, read: inter-beat durations track vowel-to-vowel intervals; Bora presupposed two-tone; no word on stress) and Seifart et al. 2018 R. Soc. Open Sci. (downloaded open via Europe PMC full-text XML, read: 'Bora is a two-tone language, i.e. every syllable is associated with either high or low tone', light/heavy mora distinction; 'stress' appears only in the general literature review) are prosody-but-not-word-stress; the 2018 paper confirms the two-tone basis of the classification, the 2012 paper is silent. Seifart & Meyer 2010 is an unpublished DGfS talk with no locatable text (Glottolog record. The only first-hand word-stress statement read is Roe 2014 (already held by the project from the 9/16 check), pp. 79 and 100: 'mixed tone/stress system', penultimate stress in 2-3-syllable words, antepenultimate in longer words, 'Tone is the only indicator of stress in Bora' — a reanalysis that refines, not supersedes, the deciding source. no reclassification indicated.

new_statements.quote: As mentioned in Chapter 1, Bora has a mixed tone/stress system. In addition to the underlying tone pattern of the noun root, Bora assigns low tones to stressed syllables. (Tone is the only indicator of stress in Bora.) ... Two and three syllable nouns have low tone on the penultimate syllable, which I analyze as a stress marker. [p. 79] ... In Bora, low tones associate to stressed syllables. Two and three syllable words have penultimate stress, while words longer than three syllables have antepenultimate stress. OCP conflicts occur when stressed syllables are adjacent to low-toned syllables. Word-medially, Bora resolves these conflicts by deleting the low stress marker. [p. 100]

Her acoustic chapter measures correlates of H vs L tone, not of stressed vs unstressed syllables, so this is an analytic reinterpretation of the same facts Thiesen & Weber describe, i.e. exactly the 'stress system implemented on tone' possibility their deciding quote leaves open. It refines rather than overturns the catalog's 'tonal' coding; the three works with stress in the title add nothing on word stress (two are silent or confirm two-tone, one is an unlocatable talk).

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's classification of Bora as tonal with no separate word stress. This endnote is the original of the sentence repeated verbatim as note 8 (p. 98) of Thiesen & Weber 2012, i.e. exactly the 'stress system implemented on tone' option that the existing Roe 2014 statement takes up; it does not itself assert penultimate/antepenultimate stress, so relative to Roe it is compatible but less committal. downloaded from the CORE mirror (https://core.ac.uk/download/235075166.pdf) because the UND Commons PDF returned an automated-access block could not be reached by automated download and direct download and web.archive.org is could not be reached by automated download.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bora is a two-tone (H/L) language in which every syllable carries H or L; the authors find no stress system separate from tone (no stressed vs. unstressed syllables), while explicitly leaving open that the tone system could be a stress system realized as tone. Tonal facts that bear on position: adjacent L tones are avoided, and suffix-assigned L tones usually land on the host's penultimate or final syllable (p. 1).
new_statements.exceptions: Note 11 (p. 21): small clan-dialect differences, mostly in palatalization, with some tone differences 'meriting further study'; Miraña's tone system 'virtually identical' (Seifart); the related language Muinane (not Bora) is said (Maxwell p.c.) to have a pitch accent system.
new_statements.identity_note: Thiesen 1996 describes Peruvian Bora (prologue: Ampiyacu, Yaguasyacu, Momón and Putumayo speakers). Weber & Thiesen 2001 covers Bora of Colombia and Peru and notes small clan-dialect tone differences and that Miraña (Colombia; Seifart's variety) has a virtually identical tone system; its remark that Muinane has a pitch accent system concerns a different language. Seifart & Meyer 2010 presumably concerns Colombian Bora/Miraña drum communication but was not opened.

new_statements.quote: Los tonos son dos: alto y bajo. El tono alto se indica con una tilde sobre la vocal, y el tono bajo no se marca. Todas las sílabas llevan un tono alto o un tono bajo. Lo que es importante es el nivel y no la fuerza de la voz. El número de sílabas con tonos altos que puede tener una palabra es ilimitado. Por el contrario, el número de sílabas con tonos bajos es limitado; pues no puede haber dos sílabas seguidas con tonos bajos, excepto al final de una palabra. [...] El tono es muy importante en el idioma bora, porque en muchos casos las formas gramaticales se distinguen solamente por el tono.
new_statements.translation: There are two tones: high and low. High tone is indicated by an acute accent over the vowel, and low tone is left unmarked. Every syllable bears either a high or a low tone. What matters is the pitch level and not the force of the voice. The number of syllables with high tone a word can have is unlimited. By contrast, the number of syllables with low tone is limited, since there cannot be two consecutive low-toned syllables except at the end of a word. [...] Tone is very important in the Bora language, because in many cases grammatical forms are distinguished only by tone.

readall_conflicts: No factual disagreement. Weber & Thiesen 2001 (note 9, p. 21; repeated as note 8, p. 98 of the 2012 grammar) say Bora has no stress system apart from its two-tone system while explicitly allowing a 'stress system implemented on tone'; Thiesen 1996 (p. 15) says pitch level, not force of voice, is what matters. The existing Roe 2014 statement reinterprets the positional L tones as penultimate (2-3 syllables) / antepenultimate (longer words) 'stress' realized only by L tone; that is an analytic choice within the option Weber & Thiesen leave open, not a contradiction of the tonal facts, and no opened source places intensity-based word stress anywhere. The unopened Seifart & Meyer 2010 talk cannot be weighed.

sources.quote: According to previous publications, Manguaré drums emulate formulaic sentences and each beat represents the tones of a syllable (Bora having two contrastive tones (H and L)) [10]. ... Bora language has six phonemic vowels positions in addition to a phonemic distinction of vowel length ... The syllable structure of Bora is (C)V(C) ... The four main syllable types are thus (C)V, (C)Vː, (C)Vh, and (C)Vʔ [11]. ... we showed that the inter-beat durations played by the Bora drummers corresponded to V-to-V intervals rather than to syllables of the associated spoken utterances.
sources.locator: sec. 1.2 'The Manguaré drummed form and the Bora language', p. 687–688; sec. 3.2 and Conclusion, p. 689–690
sources.note: Nothing on word stress or accent placement. The paper is a durational (inter-beat interval) study of the manguaré drummed form of Bora; it presupposes Bora as a two-tone (H/L) language, measures vowel-to-vowel interval durations (V < VC < VV/CCV) and an effect of the tonal duplet (LH shortest, LL/HL longest) on inter-beat duration. 'Rhythm' in the title means segmental timing, not metrical stress. The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur in the paper.

tone.says: Bora nominal lexicon shows derivation by tone change: shifting the tone within a word (to the penultimate syllable) derives a pejorative form of the root (e.g. núúmiho 'ear'); first-hand lexical/grammatical tone data on body-part nouns.

sources.citation: Seifart, Frank & Juan Alvaro Echeverri. 2015. Proto Bora-Muinane. LIAMES: Línguas Indígenas Americanas 15(2): 279-311. doi:10.20396/liames.v15i2.8642303
sources.note: P. 281: 'Note that both Bora and Muinane have phonological tone (high vs. low), although tone appears to have a relatively low functional load in both languages, at least with respect to distinguishing lexical items. Tones are for the most part associated with suffixes, which often bear floating tones that dock on the ultimate or penultimate syllable of their host, and grammatical processes like nominalization (Thiesen & Weber 2012). In the current paper, we do not attempt to reconstruct tone, but we annotate tone values (acute accent for high tone, low tone unmarked) as given in the sources…
